West Hartford by the numbers

Where is West Hartford and how is the town laid out?

West Hartford is a town in Hartford County, Connecticut, about 5 miles west of downtown Hartford. It covers 22.3 square miles and had 64,083 residents in the 2020 census.

The town borders Bloomfield, Newington, New Britain, Farmington and Avon. The Metacomet Ridge runs along the west side, and the town website lists the highest point at 778 feet on Talcott (Avon) Mountain. Town Hall sits at 120 feet.

Most people know the town by its centers. West Hartford Center is the old commercial hub around Farmington Avenue and South and North Main Street. Elmwood is the southeast section that grew up around the railroad and factories, and Interstate 84 was built through town by 1969, which cut Elmwood off from the rest. Bishops Corner opened as a shopping district in 1971, and Westfarms Mall sits on the southwest edge beside I-84.

For a seller, this means two houses a mile apart can sit in very different pockets. A street near the Center, an Elmwood block and a ridge-side lot each draw a different buyer pool, and a cash buyer prices each one on its own condition.

What in West Hartford's history explains its housing stock?

West Hartford was settled around 1679 and became its own town on May 3, 1854, after being a parish of Hartford. Most of the housing came much later, in three waves.

  • Streetcar suburbs. Trolley lines reached the countryside in 1889, and subdivisions such as Buena Vista (1895) and Elmhurst (1901) followed.
  • The 1920s. West Hill was planned in that decade with design restrictions and is a National Historic District, and the town grew from 4,808 residents in 1910 to 24,941 in 1930.
  • The postwar boom. The population went from 33,776 in 1940 to 62,382 in 1960, and the town built one new elementary school each year during the 1950s.

West Hartford was also the first Connecticut municipality to adopt zoning, in 1924. Older zoning rules and old additions can complicate a sale, so have any past permits handy.

Who bills and collects property tax in West Hartford?

The Tax Office at Town Hall bills and collects West Hartford property tax. It is at 50 South Main Street, Room 109, and answers at 860-561-7474, option 4, Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

ItemWhat the Tax Office states
Billing scheduleBills are mailed twice a year, in mid-to-late June and mid-to-late December
First installmentDue July 1, 2026; last day to pay without penalty is August 3, 2026

Motor vehicle mill rate32.46, for bills due July 1, 2026 and January 1, 2027

The office has a Delinquent Tax Collector on staff for unpaid bills. The town also uses TaxServ Capital Services, but only for delinquent motor vehicle and business personal property tax, so a house payoff is handled by the town office. You can read the Tax Office page for current figures and the FAQ page for penalty and relief questions.

How do the two installments matter when you sell?

A sale in West Hartford has to account for whichever installment is open on the closing date. The Tax Office bills the first half in summer and the second half in winter, so a closing in the spring or fall usually has one installment still ahead.

Before you sign, ask the office for a written balance on the property. Tell them the expected closing date and ask what is paid, what is open, and whether anything sits with the Delinquent Tax Collector. The Tax Office lists a Look Up My Tax Info tool and a refund request form, which help if a bill was paid twice or a bank was supposed to pay it.

The FAQ page also has a question for owners whose bank pays the tax. If a mortgage servicer handles your escrow, confirm with both the servicer and the office that the same bill is not paid twice. With a cash sale and no mortgage, the title company usually pays open tax from your proceeds, and the figure should match what the office quotes.

What can you challenge, and where do assessment questions go?

Assessment questions in West Hartford go to the town's Assessment Office, not the Tax Office. We could not open the Assessment Office page, so we do not state its appeal deadline here, and you should ask that office for the current date and form.

The Tax Office does list a page titled How Revaluation Impacts Taxes, which is worth reading if your bill changed sharply. Ask the office whether a pending appeal changes the due date on your bill.

What does the state require when a West Hartford house is sold?

Connecticut requires the seller to file a real estate conveyance tax return, Form OP-236, when the deed is recorded. The state tax is due when the price is $2,000 or more, unless an exemption applies.

  • The grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent files the return and pays the tax when the deed is recorded.
  • West Hartford's town code on the state form is 155.
  • Filing can be electronic through myCTREC for participating towns, with payment drawn only after the deed is recorded at the town clerk.
  • If the town does not take electronic filing, both pages of the form go to the town clerk with a check to the Commissioner of Revenue Services.

The state lists several exemptions. Two matter to stressed sellers. One covers a principal residence sold for a price too low to pay the mortgages plus the real estate tax and other liens that rank ahead of them. Another covers a principal residence conveyed in lieu of foreclosure. A third covers a principal residence with a pyrrhotite-damaged foundation, but only with an engineer's written evaluation. Ask your closing attorney which code applies. The DRS conveyance tax page has the full list.

Who employs West Hartford residents, and what does that mean for sellers?

The largest employers in West Hartford are the Town itself and the University of Hartford, each in the 1,100 to 2,250 range, according to the town's 2025 annual financial report as summarized on Wikipedia.

RankEmployerEmployees
1Town of West Hartford1,100 to 2,250
2University of Hartford1,100 to 2,250
3Hartford Healthcare At Home500 to 999
4Triumph Engine Control Systems250 to 499
5Connecticut Veterinary Center250 to 499

The University of Saint Joseph is also in town. The town reported a 2018 median household income of $99,280. The sellers who call us usually have an inherited house, a tenant problem, a long repair list or a tax bill that has fallen behind.

How do roads, transit, schools and utilities affect a West Hartford sale?

Interstate 84 crosses West Hartford, which gives most addresses quick access to Hartford. Connecticut Transit runs several routes along Albany, New Britain, Park, Farmington and Asylum Avenues. CTfastrak serves the town at the Elmwood and Flatbush Avenue stations. A Hartford Line stop at Flatbush Avenue has been planned, but Wikipedia notes there is not enough funding to build it.

The public system has two high schools, Conard and Hall, three middle schools and 11 elementary schools. Utilities are Eversource for electricity, the Metropolitan District for water and Connecticut Natural Gas for gas.

Buyers will ask about the heating system and the age of the roof, since the town is in the Northeast and many houses were built in the postwar years. A cash buyer accounts for those items in the offer, so you do not have to fix them first.

Call the West Hartford Tax Office at 860-561-7474, option 4. The office is in Town Hall at 50 South Main Street, Room 109, and is open Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

The Tax Office page lists 46.77 for real estate and business personal property and 32.46 for motor vehicles. The vehicle rate applies to bills due July 1, 2026 and January 1, 2027.

When is the last day to pay the July bill without penalty?

The last day for the first installment due July 1, 2026 is August 3, 2026. The second installment is due January 1, 2027, and no later than the first business day in February.

Do I have to file anything with the state when I sell?

Yes. The seller files Form OP-236 with the town clerk when the deed is recorded, and the state conveyance tax is due when the price is $2,000 or more, unless an exemption applies. West Hartford's town code is 155.

Can I sell a West Hartford house that owes back tax?

Yes. Ask the Tax Office for a written payoff figure before closing. The title company can pay open tax from the proceeds, so you do not need cash up front.

Stamford by the numbers

How large is Stamford, and why does that matter for property tax?

Stamford is Connecticut's largest city by area and, with 135,470 residents in the 2020 census, its second most populous after Bridgeport. It sits in Fairfield County on Long Island Sound, about 34 miles from New York City and 79 miles from Hartford.

The city covers 52.03 square miles, but only 37.62 of those are land. The other 14.41 square miles are water, which includes harbor, shoreline and several islands such as Cove Island and Grass Island. A city this big, with this much waterfront, bills a wide range of properties, from downtown to the shoreline to North Stamford above the Merritt Parkway.

That variety is why two Stamford houses of the same size can carry very different tax bills. Always look up the bill for your own parcel instead of using a citywide average.

Which neighborhoods make up Stamford?

Stamford has about 45 distinct neighborhoods and villages and two historic districts. The ones named most often include these.

  • Downtown, the South End and Harbor Point, the waterfront redevelopment
  • Shippan, Cove and Waterside along the Sound
  • Glenbrook and Springdale, which also have their own commuter rail stops
  • Turn of River, Newfield, Belltown, Ridgeway and Westover
  • North Stamford, the largest and least dense section, above the Merritt Parkway

Stamford borders Greenwich to the west, Darien to the east, New Canaan to the northeast and Pound Ridge, New York to the north. Because Greenwich and Darien are neighbors, sellers sometimes compare Stamford tax bills with theirs. The comparison is only useful if you check each town's current mill rate and assessment, which the city assessor and the neighboring towns publish.

What drives Stamford's economy and its tax base?

Corporate headquarters and financial services anchor the Stamford economy. As of 2023 the city was home to eight Fortune 500 companies, and it holds what Wikipedia calls the largest financial district in the New York region outside New York City.

Companies with headquarters or major operations in the city include Charter Communications, Philip Morris International, Synchrony Financial, Indeed, United Rentals, Gartner, Pitney Bowes and Crane Co. NBC Sports Group has its world headquarters here, and the Harbor Point project in the South End is described as one of the largest private-sector development projects in the country.

A large commercial grand list helps spread the cost of city services, but it also means residential owners should not assume their bill follows a regional pattern. Real estate in Stamford is valued parcel by parcel by the Assessor's Office.

What does Stamford's climate mean for a house and its value?

Stamford has a temperate coastal climate with hot summers and cold, variable winters. It averages about 30 inches of snow a year, compared with 45 to 60 inches in inland areas such as Hartford.

Hurricanes and tropical storms have made landfall on the Connecticut coast in 1903, 1938, 1944, 1954, 1960, 1985 (Gloria) and 2012 (Sandy). For a waterfront or low-lying property, that history is the reason flood zone status, flood insurance and storm damage repair come up in nearly every sale conversation.

If storm or fire damage has changed your house, ask the Assessor's Office whether and how that can affect the assessment, and ask before the bill arrives.

What are the key facts about Stamford property taxes?

Stamford's tax offices and due dates are listed at the top of this page. The table below adds the state rules that apply to every Connecticut sale and tells you where to confirm the local numbers.

We did not open a current Stamford page for the mill rate or the grievance deadline, so we leave both out. Call the city offices before you make a decision that depends on them.

How does the state's conveyance tax work on a Stamford sale?

When a deed is recorded in Stamford, the seller must file a Connecticut Real Estate Conveyance Tax Return. The Department of Revenue Services says the grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent files Form OP-236, and the filing is due when the deed is recorded.

The tax applies when the consideration is $2,000 or more, and a sale using more than one deed is taxed on the total price. Participating town clerks accept electronic filing through myCTREC.

Two exemptions are worth knowing. A principal residence conveyed in lieu of foreclosure is exempt, and so is a principal residence sold for less than the mortgages plus the real estate taxes and municipal liens that rank ahead of them. A third exemption applies to certain sellers who were approved for state or local tax relief for the elderly or disabled, though the municipal portion still applies. Your closing attorney should confirm which code to enter.

What happens to Stamford property tax when you sell?

Taxes owed on the property are paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and the title or closing attorney arranges the payoff. If the current installment is not yet due or has not been billed, the attorney normally prorates it between you and the buyer.

The state's collection chapter spells out what happens if taxes are left unpaid. It includes sections on interest on delinquent installments, demand and levy, and the method of selling real estate for taxes. It also says a tax becomes uncollectible after fifteen years. Another section allows a town to add municipal expenses to a tax bill when a property violates health, safety or housing codes, so ask whether any code enforcement charge is attached to your address.

Sellers who are behind on tax often also have a mortgage in arrears, a lien from a contractor or an estate that has not been settled. Putting all payoff figures on one sheet, with the Tax Collector's written payoff and the lender's, shows you what the sale can realistically net.

How do Stamford's schools, transit and location affect value?

Stamford is on Metro-North's New Haven Line, and its station is the second busiest on the system after Grand Central Terminal. Amtrak's Acela and Northeast Regional trains also stop there. Interstate 95 and the Merritt Parkway run through the city.

Stamford Public Schools had 16,212 students in the 2022 to 2023 school year, across 13 elementary schools, five middle schools and three high schools: Westhill, Stamford High and the Academy of Information Technology and Engineering. UConn Stamford operates a campus downtown.

Glenbrook and Springdale have their own commuter rail stops on the New Canaan branch, which gives sellers there a transit point to mention.

More questions about Stamford, CT Property Tax Guide

Who bills property tax in Stamford, Connecticut?

The city's Assessor's Office values property and the Office of the Tax Collector bills and collects the tax. Confirm current due dates and the mill rate directly with those offices.

Can I sell a Stamford house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The balance, including interest, is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and the closing attorney requests a written payoff from the Tax Collector.

What is the Stamford town code on the conveyance tax form?

The Department of Revenue Services lists 135 as the Stamford code on Form OP-236.

Does Connecticut tax the transfer of a house?

Yes. A real estate conveyance tax is due when the deed is recorded and the price is $2,000 or more, unless an exemption applies. The seller's side files the return.

Is a house sold for less than the debt exempt from the state conveyance tax?

A principal residence is exempt when the price is not enough to pay the mortgages plus the real estate taxes and municipal liens that have priority. The seller claims the exemption on the return.

How big is Stamford?

The city covers 52.03 square miles, of which 37.62 are land, and had 135,470 residents in the 2020 census. It is Connecticut's largest city by area.

New Haven by the numbers

Where is New Haven and how is the city laid out?

New Haven sits on New Haven Harbor, on the northern shore of Long Island Sound, in New Haven County. The city covers about 20.1 square miles, of which roughly 1.4 square miles is water, and the 2020 census counted 134,023 residents.

The street plan dates to 1638, when the settlers laid out eight streets in a three-by-three grid known as the Nine Square Plan. The 16-acre New Haven Green is the middle square, and the plan is still visible downtown. Two reddish trap rock ridges, East Rock and West Rock, rise to the northeast and northwest of the core, and three rivers drain the city: the West, the Mill and the Quinnipiac.

Wikipedia's neighborhood list gives a sense of how many separate markets sit inside one city limit:

  • Downtown, Dwight and Dixwell near the center
  • The Hill, City Point and Long Wharf along the southern harbor
  • East Rock, Newhallville and Prospect Hill on the north side
  • Wooster Square, Fair Haven and Mill River in the east central area
  • Westville, Edgewood, Beaver Hills and West River to the west
  • The Annex and East Shore (Morris Cove) facing the harbor

A house in Westville and a house in the Hill can carry very different assessments, repair needs and buyer pools, even though both receive the same kind of city tax bill.

What does the New Haven economy mean for a seller?

Yale University is New Haven's largest employer and, according to Wikipedia, its biggest taxpayer. Yale New Haven Hospital comes next, followed by Southern Connecticut State University, the Assa Abloy lock business, the Knights of Columbus headquarters and United Illuminating. Services make up about 56 percent of the local economy.

That mix matters for property tax, since a single institution is the largest taxpayer. Connecticut abolished county government in 1960, which means there is no county tax bill here. The city bills for municipal services, schools and everything else in one place.

The Census Bureau survey figures summarized above show about 72 percent of occupied homes in New Haven are rented, so a good share of sellers here own rental property.

When are New Haven property taxes due and how do you pay?

New Haven bills real estate tax on a July 1 to June 30 fiscal year, with the first payment due July 1 and the second due January 1. The Tax Collector's page says the city sends only one bill, usually mailed in June, and that taxes are payable in advance.

ItemWhat the city page says
First installmentDue July 1, covers July 1 to December 31
Second installmentDue January 1, covers January 1 to June 30
Bills mailedOne bill, typically in June
In personOffice of the Tax Collector, 165 Church St, 1st floor, Monday to Friday 9 AM to 5 PM
MailCollector of Taxes, City of New Haven, PO Box 1927, New Haven, CT 06509-1927

The city asks mailers to write the tax account number on the check. Online payments made before 8 PM Monday to Thursday post the next business day, while later ones can take 48 hours or more. If a deadline is close, pay by cash, money order or bank check so there is no hold.

The office page does not list a penalty rate, so confirm the current interest charge with the Tax Collector before you rely on any figure. Our source page is the city's own.

What happens to the tax bill when a New Haven house sells?

The city tells new homebuyers that after closing, the buyer is responsible for the next bill that becomes due, either the July 1 or the January 1 installment. The city page sends buyers to the closing attorney for questions about how the current period is split.

Several state rules can touch a sale. The Connecticut General Assembly's Chapter 204 lists a section on receipts for partial payments when property is transferred, and another on municipal expenses added to the tax bill for real estate that violates health, safety or housing codes. A separate section lets a municipality abate tax that exceeds 8 percent of an owner's income. Under that option the owner signs a reimbursement agreement that is recorded as a lien and becomes due in full when the property is sold or the last owner dies.

Before you list or accept a cash offer, ask your attorney or title company to pull a current tax status for each installment, any code-enforcement charges and any recorded abatement lien.

How does New Haven weather affect an older house?

New Haven has hot, humid summers and cool to cold winters with both rain and snow. Wikipedia notes that temperatures top 80 degrees Fahrenheit on about 70 days a year, and the harbor setting means storms can hit hard. The 1938 hurricane, Hurricane Carol in 1954 and Hurricane Gloria in 1985 all struck the city.

For a seller, that history points to a few checks:

  • Roof and gutter condition after wind-driven rain
  • Basement moisture in low areas near the West, Mill and Quinnipiac rivers and the shoreline
  • Heating systems that can handle mixed freeze and thaw winters
  • Whether a flood zone map applies to the lot, which your title company or lender can confirm

We have not confirmed a flood zone designation for any specific New Haven street here, so ask the city or your insurer for the parcel in question.

Which schools, colleges and roads shape demand in New Haven?

New Haven Public Schools serves the city, and Wilbur Cross High School and Hillhouse High School are its two largest public high schools. Hopkins School, founded in 1660, is a private school. Higher education includes Yale, Southern Connecticut State University, Albertus Magnus College and Gateway Community College, which has a downtown campus.

The Wilbur Cross Parkway passes through a tunnel under West Rock, the only highway tunnel through a natural obstacle in Connecticut. Tweed New Haven Airport serves the region. Buyers who work at the universities or the hospital often look for homes close to those campuses, which is one reason pockets such as East Rock and Westville draw different offers than neighborhoods farther from the center.

What are the options if you owe New Haven property tax and want to sell?

You can sell a house in New Haven even if taxes are unpaid, because the unpaid amount is paid from the sale proceeds at closing. The practical steps are short:

  • Ask the Tax Collector for the exact balance by installment and tax account number.
  • Ask the Assessor's Office whether any appeal or correction is pending.
  • Have your closing attorney confirm any liens or code charges.
  • Compare a cash offer against the cost of fixing the house and carrying it through another installment.

A cash buyer that purchases as-is saves you repairs and showings, though it is smart to read any offer closely and ask a lawyer about it.

The first installment is due July 1 and the second is due January 1. New Haven mails a single bill, usually in June, and the fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30.

Where do I pay New Haven property tax in person?

Pay at the Office of the Tax Collector, 165 Church St, 1st floor, Monday to Friday 9 AM to 5 PM. The office takes cash, check, money order or bank check but not debit or credit cards.

Who pays the tax at a New Haven closing?

The buyer is responsible for the next bill that comes due after closing, per the city's page for new homebuyers. Your closing attorney sets how the current period is divided.

Is there a county property tax in New Haven?

No. Connecticut abolished county government in 1960, so the city handles the bill for local services and schools.

Yes. The title company pays unpaid tax from the sale proceeds, so ask for a payoff figure before closing.

Where is Greenwich, Connecticut, and how large is it?

Greenwich is the southwesternmost town in Connecticut and in New England, a town of 63,518 people in the 2020 census. It borders Port Chester and Rye Brook and North Castle in New York, Stamford to the east, and Long Island Sound to the south.

The total area is 67.2 square miles, 47.8 of land and 19.4 of water, so water makes up nearly 29 percent of the town. Wikipedia notes that this is twice the size of Manhattan. ZIP codes are 06830, 06831, 06870 and 06878.

Greenwich is one town and one taxing body, but it is made of distinct sections, and that matters when a buyer asks where a house sits.

  • The Census Bureau recognizes nine places inside the town: Byram, Cos Cob, Glenville, Indian Field, Old Greenwich, Pemberwick, Riverside, Rock Ridge and the central Greenwich area.
  • Cos Cob, Old Greenwich and Riverside have their own postal names and ZIP codes.
  • Informal areas include the Back Country, Mid-Country, Belle Haven, Chickahominy, Mianus, Banksville and the Fourth Ward.

What is the history of Greenwich?

Agents Robert Feake and Daniel Patrick bought the land from the Siwanoy in 1640 for 25 English coats, on behalf of the New Haven Colony. The Connecticut General Assembly declared Greenwich a township on May 11, 1665.

General Israel Putnam made his well-known escape from British forces in Greenwich on February 26, 1779. The town also has a 2001 landmark in beach law: after Leydon v. Greenwich, the town had to open all four of its beaches, including Greenwich Point, to non-residents.

Those four beaches on the Sound are Greenwich Point, Byram Beach, Island Beach and Great Captain Island, which includes the southernmost point in Connecticut.

What drives the Greenwich economy?

Finance dominates. Greenwich is home to many hedge funds and financial services firms, drawn by a residential setting close to Manhattan, according to Wikipedia.

The list above names examples and is not a ranking by headcount.

How does Greenwich weather affect a house?

Greenwich has a humid continental climate that sits close to humid subtropical. Average annual precipitation is 50.45 inches, and average snowfall is 28 inches a year.

Snow is not even across town. Wikipedia reports that the area north of the Merritt Parkway usually gets heavier snowfall than the coast, where Long Island Sound moderates winter weather. January highs average 35 degrees and July highs 82.

  • Areas north of the Merritt Parkway, such as the Back Country, can see more snow than the shoreline.
  • Coastal sections such as Old Greenwich, Riverside and Byram sit near the water, so flood zone status is a standard question for buyers.

We did not open an official Greenwich page on flood or zoning rules. The town's Planning and Zoning and Wetlands offices can answer for a specific address.

How do trains, highways and schools serve Greenwich?

Metro-North's New Haven Line has four Greenwich stations: Greenwich, Cos Cob, Riverside and Old Greenwich. An express train to Grand Central takes about 50 minutes and a local about 60.

Interstate 95 crosses the south end of town with exits 2 through 5. The Boston Post Road (Route 1) and the Merritt Parkway also run through, and Westchester County Airport is about 15 minutes by car from the town center.

Greenwich Public Schools has one high school, Greenwich High School, three middle schools (Central, Eastern and Western) and eleven elementary schools, including Cos Cob, Glenville, Old Greenwich, Riverside and North Street. Wikipedia reports that about 25 to 30 percent of K-12 residents attend private schools, a high share for the region.

Greenwich bills real estate, personal property and motor vehicle tax together. The Tax Collector's page says bills were mailed June 17, payment is due July 1, and the bill is delinquent after August 3.

The office is in Town Hall, 101 Field Point Road, Room 145, open Monday to Friday from 8:30 am to 3:30 pm, and the phone is 203-622-7891.

You file with the elected Board of Assessment Appeals, not the Assessor. The Board's page says the Assessor's Office will not accept appeal forms.

  • The appeal covers the assessment only. The tax amount comes from the mill rate, which the Board of Estimate and Taxation sets in May.
  • The Board can raise, lower or leave an assessment alone, and mails decisions about two weeks after hearings end.

The seller or the seller's attorney files the state's Form OP-236 when the deed is recorded, and Greenwich's town code on that form is 057. The Department of Revenue Services says tax is due when consideration reaches $2,000 unless the transfer is exempt.

Exempt transfers on the state list include a deed in lieu of foreclosure on a principal residence, a principal residence sold for too little to cover its mortgages and tax liens, and transfers between spouses.

What do Greenwich sellers usually face?

Greenwich is a mix of coastal sections, village centers and the Back Country, so a seller's situation depends heavily on the street.

  • Houses with deferred repairs can be hard to sell on the open market.
  • Estates may need time to settle ownership before listing.

Bridgeport by the numbers

Where is Bridgeport, and who handles property tax there?

Bridgeport is the most populous city in Connecticut, with 148,654 residents in 2020, and it sits in eastern Fairfield County at the mouth of the Pequonnock River on Long Island Sound. The city is about 60 miles from Manhattan, and two City offices share the property tax work: the Tax Assessor values property and the Tax Collector bills and collects.

Bridgeport was incorporated as a town in 1821 and as a city in 1836. It runs under a mayor-council system. The city covers 19.4 square miles, of which 16.0 is land and 3.4 is water, and its elevation is only 3.3 feet, which matters for flood and storm questions later on this page.

How is Bridgeport property tax calculated?

Bridgeport multiplies the assessed value of a property by the mill rate, and one mill equals $1 of tax for each $1,000 of assessment. For fiscal year 2026-2027 the city's rate is 27.95 mills on real estate and personal property.

The city's own worked example uses an assessed value of $200,000. Multiplying $200,000 by 0.02795 gives a tax of $5,590. The city's example describes the figure as the 70 percent assessed value, which means the assessed value used for tax is a share of the market value and not the full market price.

That matters when you read your bill. The assessed value on the notice is the figure the mill rate applies to, so compare it with your bill rather than with a sale price.

The mill rate history is posted on the Tax Collector's general tax information page, and the Tax Assessor's page explains how taxes are determined.

When are Bridgeport property taxes due, and when do they go delinquent?

Bridgeport property tax is due in two installments, July 1 and January 1, and Connecticut law makes an installment delinquent if it is not paid by the first day of the next month. For the July installment that means August 1, and for the January installment it means February 1.

InstallmentDueDelinquent if unpaid after
FirstJuly 1August 1
SecondJanuary 1February 1

Under Connecticut General Statutes section 12-146, the delinquent part of the tax is charged interest at 18 percent a year from the date it was due. Each part of a month counts as a whole month, and the minimum interest charge is $2 per installment unless the municipality has voted not to impose it. Interest keeps running even after a judgment for the city.

The collector applies partial payments to interest first and principal second. A payment also counts as on time if it was made through a municipal electronic payment service in the allowed time or if the envelope carries a postmark within the allowed time.

The city files liens on June 30, the last day of the fiscal year, so ask the collector whether one has been filed against your property.

How do you appeal a Bridgeport property assessment?

You appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals, and Connecticut law says the written appeal must be filed on or before February 20. The statute allows filing in writing or by email, in the manner the board prescribes.

The appeal has to include specific items:

  • The property owner's name and the signer's name and position.
  • A description of the property.
  • A name, mailing address and email address for all correspondence.
  • The reason for the appeal and your estimate of value.
  • The owner's or authorized agent's signature and the date.

The board must tell each filer the date, time and place of the hearing no later than March 1, and the notice has to go out at least seven calendar days before the hearing. For commercial, industrial, utility or apartment property assessed above $1 million, the board may choose not to hold a hearing, and in that case the owner can go straight to Superior Court under section 12-117a.

If the assessor received an extension, the filing deadline moves to March 20 and hearings take place in April. When the board changes a gross assessment, the new figure stays fixed until the next revaluation, with limited exceptions for new construction, damage, demolition, court orders and factual corrections.

A person who received title after the assessment date may also appeal, and so may a lessee bound by a recorded lease to pay the real property taxes. Ask the Tax Assessor's office for the current year's application form.

What is Bridgeport's history, and how did it shape the housing?

Bridgeport grew as a port and factory city, and by 1905 it was Connecticut's chief manufacturing city. Between 1870 and 1910 its population climbed from about 25,000 to more than 100,000, and many of those workers were immigrants from Ireland, Slovakia, Hungary, Germany, England and Italy.

P. T. Barnum lived in the city, served as mayor in 1871 and built four houses there. Harvey Hubbell founded Hubbell Incorporated in Bridgeport in 1888. After the Second World War the AVCO Lycoming division, founded in 1951, employed at times more than 12,000 people building military hardware, and it closed in 1984. Deindustrialization hit the city hard in the 1970s and 1980s.

Since the early 21st century the city has pursued large redevelopment projects. Its crime rate fell by nearly 50 percent between 2010 and 2018, according to the Wikipedia summary of the city.

This history explains why Bridgeport has a wide spread of housing ages and conditions. The city is also home to the University of Bridgeport, Housatonic Community College, part of Sacred Heart University, three museums and the state's only zoo.

Which parts of Bridgeport might a seller hear about?

Bridgeport is divided into five geographic areas, Downtown, the East Side, the North End, the South End and the West Side, and the city's neighborhood list is organized under those names. Each area has smaller neighborhoods inside it.

The city calls itself the Park City because it has 35 public parks covering 1,300 acres. Sikorsky Memorial Airport serves the city, Route 8/25 runs toward Waterbury and Newtown, and Bridgeport Station serves commuter rail.

How do Bridgeport's climate and coastline affect a house?

Bridgeport's coastal location brings storm and flood questions that inland Connecticut towns face less often. Hurricanes and tropical storms have landed on the Connecticut coast in 1903, 1938, 1944, 1954, 1960, 1985 and, with Hurricane Sandy, in 2012.

The city averages 44.9 inches of precipitation a year and about 29 inches of snow, which is much less than inland Hartford or Albany. Snow cover of at least an inch lasts an average of 33 days each winter. The record low is 7 degrees below zero and the record high is 103 degrees.

For a seller, that history means a buyer, an insurer or a lender may ask whether the home sits in a flood zone, and it can matter for older basements, roofs and sea walls. We did not find an official Bridgeport page on flood zone disclosure that we could open, so ask your agent or title company what applies to your parcel.

A seller with unpaid Bridgeport tax should get a payoff figure from the Tax Collector before closing, because interest at 18 percent a year keeps adding to a delinquent balance. A closing agent can pay the tax from the sale proceeds if the figure is current on the closing date.

  • List which installments are unpaid, July, January or both, and which fiscal years they belong to.
  • Ask for the interest to date and the per-month amount that will be added if closing slips.
  • Check whether a lien was filed on the last June 30.
  • If you think the assessment is wrong, the February 20 appeal date is a hard line, so do not wait until the closing is scheduled.

We did not confirm a Bridgeport rule on proration of taxes between buyer and seller, so rely on your contract and your closing agent for that split.

The written appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals is due on or before February 20, or March 20 if the assessor was granted an extension.

Can a new owner appeal an assessment from before the purchase?

Yes. Section 12-111 lets a person to whom title was transferred since the assessment date appeal to the board.

Where is Norwalk, Connecticut and how big is it?

The 2020 census counted 38,152 housing units in the city, 5.4 percent of them vacant. About 29.6 percent of households were people living alone.

What are the six Norwalk taxing districts?

Norwalk has six taxing districts, and each one has its own property tax rate that reflects the services it receives from the city. This is the single most important fact for a Norwalk owner, because two houses a mile apart can carry different rates.

According to Wikipedia, the First, Second, Third and Sixth districts are political entities with their own elected officers, annual meetings and budgets. The Fourth and Fifth districts are not counted as separate governments and make up the city proper. The districts also supply utilities in parts of town:

Norwalk is a corporate address. Commuters to New York City value the rail stops, which can make a house near a station easier to market. Norwalk Public Schools operates the public schools, with Norwalk High School and Brien McMahon High School as the two largest high schools.

A Norwalk sale can pay off unpaid property tax from the proceeds. Where is Danbury and how big is it?

Danbury is a city in Fairfield County, about 50 miles northeast of New York City, with a 2020 census population of 86,518. That makes it the seventh-largest city in Connecticut, according to Wikipedia.

The city covers 44.19 square miles, of which 41.95 are land and 2.24 are water. It was incorporated as a town in 1702, became a city in 1889, and consolidated with the town government in 1965, so one set of city offices handles assessment and collection for the whole area.

Danbury is made up of named districts rather than one grid. Aqua Vista near Candlewood Lake, Beaverbrook, Beckettville, Germantown, Great Plain, Hayestown, Long Ridge, King Street, Lake Waubeeka, Mill Plain, Miry Brook, Pembroke and Wooster Heights all show up on the city's neighborhood list. Danbury is called the Hat City because it was once the center of the American hat industry. Wikipedia traces the first hat shop to 1780, when Zadoc Benedict employed three people who made 18 hats a week.

By 1800 the town was turning out 20,000 hats a year, and by 1887 thirty factories were producing 5 million. Settlers had arrived in 1685, and British troops under Major General William Tryon burned and sacked the town on April 26, 1777. Interstate 84 and U.S. Route 7 are the main highways, and they overlap through the downtown area. I-84 runs west to Westchester and the Hudson Valley and east toward Waterbury and Hartford, while Route 7 runs south to Norwalk and I-95.

The city maintains 242 miles of streets. Lake Avenue, West Street, White Street and Federal Road carry much of the surface traffic, and Routes 6, 37, 39 and 53 handle the rest.

Danbury is the end of the Metro-North Danbury Branch, which runs through South Norwalk and Stamford to Grand Central Terminal. Housatonic Area Regional Transit buses connect greater Danbury, and Danbury Municipal Airport sits in the southwest corner of the city near the mall.

That page carries a 2010 update stamp, so confirm the current installment rules with the Tax Collector before relying on it. The FAQ also says that once a deed is filed with the Town Clerk, the Assessor changes the owner name and address on the property.

Where is Fairfield, Connecticut, and how is it laid out?

Fairfield is a shoreline town in Fairfield County that borders Bridgeport, Trumbull, Easton, Weston and Westport. The 2020 census counted 61,512 residents, and Wikipedia lists a 2024 estimate of 65,300.

The town covers 31.38 square miles, with 29.9 of them land and 1.48 water, and it sits in the Greater Bridgeport Planning Region. ZIP codes are 06824, 06825 and 06828. Roger Ludlow founded the plantation in 1639.

Fairfield works as a group of sections more than one center. Named areas include Southport, Greenfield Hill, Stratfield, Tunxis Hill, the University area, Grasmere, Mill Plain, Knapp's Village, Melville Village, Holland Hill, Murray and the Fairfield Beach area. Two shopping strips, the Post Road (Route 1) and Black Rock Turnpike, tie them together.

What is the history of Fairfield?

Fairfield's best-known event is the burning of July 7, 1779, when about 2,000 British troops landed near Pine Creek Point and burned the town for its support of independence. George Washington noted the damage still visible when he passed through a decade later.

Several nearby municipalities were carved from Fairfield: Redding in 1767, Weston in 1787, Bridgeport in 1821, Westport in 1835, and Easton from Weston in 1845.

The twentieth century changed the town's character. Munitions work in Bridgeport during World War I pushed residents out to Fairfield, and the population grew from about 6,000 to 17,000 by 1929. The Connecticut Turnpike in the 1950s brought another wave, and by the 1960s the suburban pattern was set. General Electric kept its headquarters in town from about 1970 until it moved to Boston on May 8, 2017.

Fairfield has about 5 miles of Long Island Sound coastline, five lifeguarded town beaches, and several tidal waterways. Houses near water carry questions that inland houses do not.

Hamden was part of New Haven until 1786, when about 1,400 residents incorporated it as a separate town named for the English statesman John Hampden. The Quinnipiac people were the first inhabitants, and the land was bought for the New Haven Colony in 1638.

Eli Whitney made arms for the U.S. government at a Hamden mill site beginning in 1798 and used interchangeable parts there. The stone houses he built for workers in Whitneyville are described as the first employer-provided housing in the country. The dam he enlarged in 1806 created Lake Whitney.

How is Meriden property tax billed and when is it due?

Meriden's Tax Collector bills real estate tax once a year in July, but lets owners pay the real estate bill in four equal installments due in July, October, January and April. Bills are mailed only once, so keep the bill for the remaining installments.

The city's page uses the 2023 grand list and the July 1, 2024 due date as its example, so confirm the current year with the office. The first payment must be made by August 1 to avoid the late charge. After that, interest runs at 1.5% per month, or 18% per year, from July 1. Meriden waives interest for July as a grace period, and the minimum charge after that is 3% or $2.00, whichever is greater.

What does Meriden's citywide revaluation mean for owners?

Meriden revalued all real estate for the October 1, 2025 grand list, and the new values feed tax bills due beginning in July 2026. The city hired Vision Government Solutions, a state-certified revaluation company, to help the assessor.

Appraisers studied property sales in the 24 months before October 1, 2025 to see where values rose or fell, then applied those findings to homes that had not sold. Residential data mailers were sent so owners could confirm details, and inspections were possible for recent sales, open building permits or random quality checks.

Data collectors carry photo ID, and the city says they will not enter a house unless an adult is present and gives permission for an interior inspection. If you are selling soon, check your property record card for errors, because wrong square footage or a wrong bathroom count flows straight into the assessment. The city's revaluation page has the details.

What happens in Meriden if property tax or water bills go unpaid?

Meriden places a lien on real estate when tax stays unpaid past the end of the year in which it was due, and the city may later foreclose on that lien. Property owners who receive a demand letter are told to respond right away.

  • Building permits are not issued for a property that has such a debt, and Neighborhood Preservation Program funding is withheld.
  • Water and sewer bills are issued and due in March, June, September and December, and unpaid bills can lead to shutoff or a recommendation for foreclosure.
  • Payment in full is preferred, but payment plans are often accepted when the account will be current within one year.
  • All motor vehicle taxes under your name must be paid before DMV clearance, even ones not yet delinquent.

A lien does not stop a sale. The closing attorney or title company pays it from the proceeds, so a seller with a recorded lien can still sell the house.

How does a Meriden sale close with back taxes, and who files the state return?

At a Meriden closing, the title company requests payoffs for tax, water and sewer, then pays them from the seller's proceeds before the deed is recorded. The Meriden town clerk records the deed. Meriden's code on the Department of Revenue Services list is 080.

The seller or the seller's attorney files Form OP-236, the Connecticut real estate conveyance tax return, when the deed is recorded. See the state's conveyance tax information. Exemptions exist for a principal residence transferred in lieu of foreclosure and for one where the price cannot cover the mortgages and priority tax liens.

Where is West Haven and what are its neighborhoods?

West Haven is a city in New Haven County on the coast of Long Island Sound, with 55,584 residents in the 2020 census. It covers 10.92 square miles, or about 5,171 people per square mile.

The Oyster River separates it from Milford on the southwest. Orange lies to the northwest, New Haven to the north, and the West River runs along the northeast edge. New Haven Harbor is to the east and the Sound to the south.

The city has 3.5 miles of publicly accessible beach, which Wikipedia says is about a quarter of the public beach in Connecticut. For a seller, location in one of these areas shapes the likely buyer, and houses near the water are a different product from a hillside house in Allingtown.

What is the history behind West Haven's housing?

West Haven was settled in 1648 as West Farms, part of the New Haven Colony, and became a separate parish in 1719. It split from Orange to become its own town in 1921 and was incorporated as a city in 1961, which is why it calls itself Connecticut's youngest city.

Savin Rock was a seaside resort by the 1870s and later an amusement park that closed in the 1960s. A long redevelopment fight followed, and the area is now parks and shoreline open space under a conservation easement signed in 2007.

The city grew from 25,808 residents in 1930 to 43,002 in 1960 and 52,851 in 1970. Houses from those decades are now old enough that roofs, wiring and heating systems are fair questions for any buyer.

Who assesses and bills property tax in West Haven?

The Assessor's Office values property, and the Tax Collector bills and collects. The Assessor's Office is in City Hall at 355 Main Street, 1st floor, and can be reached at 203-937-3515. Hours are Monday to Friday from 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

The Assessor's page offers a street list by fire district, and the mill rates are posted as a separate sheet. We have not confirmed the current rates, so we do not print one. What does the state require when a West Haven house is sold?

The seller files Connecticut Form OP-236 when the deed is recorded, and the state tax is due when the price is $2,000 or more unless an exemption applies. West Haven's town code on the state form is 156.

  • The grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent files the return.
  • Participating towns can use the state's myCTREC portal, and the payment is drawn only after recording.
  • Towns that do not take electronic filing receive both pages of the form and a check to the Commissioner of Revenue Services.

The state also lists an exemption for a principal residence sold for too little to pay the mortgages plus the real estate tax and other liens ahead of them, and another for a principal residence deeded in lieu of foreclosure. Your closing attorney should pick the right code. The DRS conveyance tax page lists all of them.

Who works in West Haven and what changed in the local economy?

West Haven was a shipping and manufacturing city, with buckle shops in the Civil War era, Armstrong Rubber in World War II and later Coleco and Sikorsky operations. Bayer closed its plant in 2006, affecting about 1,000 workers, and Yale bought the 137-acre campus in 2007 for life sciences research.

Today the University of New Haven, a U.S. Veterans Affairs hospital and Yale's athletic fields and West Campus are part of the picture. The city's 2020 median household income was $73,566, and it had 22,735 housing units, 5.8% of them vacant. Wikipedia does not list a current top-employer table, so we do not rank employers here.

How do roads, transit and schools affect a West Haven sale?

Interstate 95, Route 34 and U.S. Route 1 run through West Haven, along with Routes 162 and 122. The Connecticut DOT opened a Metro-North station on the New Haven Line in 2013, with 660 parking spaces. Amtrak does not stop in West Haven, and the closest stop is New Haven's Union Station.

CT Transit New Haven buses serve Campbell Avenue and the shore. Tweed New Haven Regional Airport is the nearest airport with air service. The public school system has one high school, a middle school, an intermediate school and six elementary schools.

It can. Wikipedia reports that the two remaining independent fire districts each levy their own rate, and the Assessor posts a street list by fire district. Ask the Tax Collector which applies to your address.

Where is Manchester, Connecticut, and how big is it?

Manchester is a town in Hartford County, about 10 miles east of Hartford's Union Station, with 59,713 residents in the 2020 census. It covers 27.7 square miles, and its urban center, the Manchester census-designated place, takes up roughly 23% of that area.

Manchester is a town with a council-manager government, so the same Town of Manchester offices assess, bill and collect property tax for every neighborhood inside its borders. ZIP codes in town run 06040 to 06042 and 06045.

What is Manchester's history, and why does it matter to houses here?

Manchester grew from a farming and mill area into one of the largest silk-making towns in the country, and that history is why so many older homes sit near the old mill district. Colonists settled the area around 1673, and the Cheney family started what became the world's largest silk mill in 1838.

The Cheney Brothers Historic District is a National Historic Landmark. Its mills, owners' houses and workers' homes survive, and some mills now hold apartments. Wikipedia also notes that the Pitkin Glassworks ran from 1783 to 1830 and that the Hilliard woolen mill site is the oldest in the country.

For a seller, the practical point is age. Houses built for mill workers and the neighborhoods that grew around them are now a century or more old, which usually means old wiring, plumbing and roofs that a buyer will price in.

Manchester contains parts of three interstates: I-84, I-384 and I-291. Route 6 and Route 44 run together as the main east-west road, Route 30 crosses the north of town, and Route 83 is the principal north-south road, running as South Main Street and then Main Street.

  • Connecticut Transit routes 80, 82, 83, 84, 85, 88 and 121 connect Manchester with Hartford.
  • There is no passenger rail service in town. The closest is Hartford's Union Station, about 10 miles west.
  • Bradley International Airport in Windsor Locks is the main commercial airport nearby.
  • The Charter Oak Greenway and the Hop River State Park Trail are the best-known bike routes.

With three interstates and direct bus links, a Manchester house is easy to reach from Hartford, which widens the pool of people who might want it.

Which schools, parks and services come with a Manchester address?

Manchester High School and Howell Cheney Technical High School serve grades 9 to 12, and the town also has two magnet schools, Great Path Academy and Discovery Academy. East Catholic High School is the Catholic option, and Manchester Community College is a two-year college inside the town.

Outdoor space includes the 53-acre Oak Grove Nature Center at Wickham Park, Case Mountain Recreation Area in the southeast corner and Charter Oak Park downtown, which had a $2 million renovation in 2017. Buyers who want trails or parks nearby often start with those.

  • The Manchester Fire Department runs from seven firehouses after the Eighth Utilities District merged into it on July 1, 2023.
  • The Manchester Road Race, first run in 1927, takes place every Thanksgiving morning and draws more than 10,000 participants.

Data collection and market analysis began in early 2026 and runs through September 2026, with mailers sent to residential owners and visits to some parcels, especially recent purchases and homes with permitted work. Valuation follows. Notices of new values were scheduled for the fall of 2026, and informal meetings with assessment staff come after that.

The town uses Tyler Technologies as its revaluation company. If you plan to sell, read your notice and use the informal meeting to correct any wrong details on your property record. You can find the page on the town's revaluation overview.

Tax not paid on or before August 1 becomes delinquent and carries interest at 1.5% per month back to the original due date. To avoid interest, a payment must be postmarked by August 1. Any delinquent tax carries a minimum interest charge of $2.00.

  • Not receiving a bill does not cancel the tax or the interest.
  • Taxes can be paid online, by phone at 1-844-562-1959, by mail, or in the drop box behind Town Hall (no cash in the box).

The Collector of Revenue Office at Town Hall is open Monday, Wednesday and Thursday 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM, Tuesday 8:00 AM to 7:00 PM and Friday 8:00 AM to 1:00 PM, per the town's 2025 notice. The phone is 860-647-3018 and the email is collector@manchesterct.gov. See the town's tax payment notice, and check that hours have not changed.

The title company or closing attorney asks the Collector of Revenue for a payoff and pays what is owed from your proceeds at closing. You do not need cash on hand ahead of time.

Route 9 runs alongside the river and bisects the city. The west side is flanked by the Metacomet Ridge, including Higby Mountain and the north side of Lamentation Mountain. Middletown shares borders with Cromwell, Portland, East Hampton, Haddam, Durham, Middlefield, Berlin and Meriden.

By the American Revolution it was a thriving port, and in the 19th century it became a manufacturing center for marine hardware, typewriters and machine tools.

Wesleyan University was founded in 1831. In 1841, the city established the state's first public high school. In 1868 the Connecticut General Hospital for the Insane opened here, and it is now Connecticut Valley Hospital, still a major employer.

Route 9 is the spine, and Interstate 91 clips the western edge. River Valley Transit serves Middletown and runs to Old Saybrook, which links to Amtrak and Shore Line East. Middletown's probate court district covers the city plus Cromwell, Portland, Middlefield and Haddam, which matters if you are selling an inherited house.

Whose name is on a Middletown tax bill after a sale?

The record owner as of the October 1 grand list date stays on the bill until the next assessment date.
